article.body:
Computers are investigating how physical systems retain information about their past states. This work begins with understanding causal memory, which is how a system's current configuration depends on its previous state. We use coarse-graining, which is an analogy to looking at a detailed picture from far away so that only the broad shapes are visible, to simplify complex systems and study their behavior. Recent work suggests that this process limits how accurately we can reconstruct a system's history because it hides the energy spent during state transitions. This implies that maintaining a reliable memory is fundamentally bounded by available energy and how much information we lose during the simplification process [1].

The research also explores how records become objective, or public facts. An objective record is one that many independent observers can agree upon, regardless of their own viewpoint. We are examining spectrum broadcast structures, which is an analogy like a radio tower broadcasting a signal in all directions so that anyone with a receiver can hear the same report. This happens when a system redundantly encodes its state into the environment, making the information accessible and robust against interference, even when quantum information scrambling threatens to delocalize or hide these details. This suggests that objective reality emerges from interactions that effectively share information rather than keeping it locked within the system [2].

We are also investigating how chemistry itself acts as a memory device. We are studying autocatalytic networks, which is an analogy like a fire that uses its own heat to keep burning, where reaction products act as catalysts to produce more of themselves. These systems can maintain persistent chemical states without requiring modern genetics or template copying. Our teams have identified algebraic conditions, which means specific mathematical formulas involving reaction components, that allow these networks to maintain their state over time. This research helps explain how early chemical environments might have held onto historical information before the evolution of life [3].

Despite this progress, we are still refining how these concepts fit together. We are trying to understand how sensitive these systems are to noise and if there is a distinct boundary where a simple, persistent state becomes a truly heritable, evolving memory. Can these different memory types—physical, environmental, and chemical—be described by a single underlying rule, or do they function under distinct, non-overlapping laws?

Summary

Our research groups studied how physical systems keep records of their past. We looked at how energy affects memory, how information spreads to become public facts, and how chemical reactions sustain themselves. We found that simplifying details helps us understand these systems but also hides information. We are still learning what defines a true memory. You can see all our ongoing records on the public Console.
article.lede: Our research teams are mapping the fundamental limits of how physical systems store information, from energetic costs to redundant environmental broadcasting and self-sustaining chemical networks.
article.lens: This editorial sequence synthesizes research across physical memory, environmental broadcasting, and autocatalytic networks to build a unified understanding of how information persists in non-equilibrium systems.
article.title: Understanding How Physical Systems Remember the Past
